This page holds the exercise of the course, Tasks 1 to 5, on a copy of R that runs inside the browser, with the data already in place and the same helper functions as the downloadable workspace. The short session and the one-day formats of the housing-audit case are worked on this page, and the facilitator drives it on the shared screen. The downloadable workspace described on the [Setup](../../setup.qmd) page holds the same tasks for anyone who has installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), and nothing done in either is wasted, since both fit the same models to the same data and give the same numbers.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## While the R engine loads

The R engine downloads into your browser the first time you open this page (10–30 seconds on a slow connection). Read Task 1 while it loads. You will know that it is ready when the first code cell switches from a loading spinner to a "Run Code" button.

Keep this tab open. Your work stays in this page until you refresh it – there is nothing to install, nothing to save to disk, and no account needed.
:::

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Lab machinery: the estimator of the course, the specification menu, its
# validation, and the helpers of Tasks 4 and 5 – try_spec(), my_experiments(),
# submit_exploration(), prereg(), run_spec() and report_result(). The same
# code as R/spec_tools.R of the downloadable workspace, apart from the tag of
# the class chart, which lasts for the browser session here. Every
# specification is fitted live; data/spec_curve.csv places it among the 64,
# and data/menu_options.csv gives the reason for every option that is not on
# the curve. Both arrive with the page through its `resources:` list.

# ============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION – the class chart and the course site
# ============================================================================
# The results Form that submit_exploration() and report_result() pre-fill: its
# ID and the entry codes of its seven fields. They belong to the Form that the
# cases of the course share, set up for the EU-frames case; a Form of its own
# replaces them here and nowhere else. The word in .case_word follows the tag
# in every label, so that the chart of this case reads only its own rows.
.form_id <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
.form_entry <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
                 t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
                 r = "entry.1660273001")
.case_word <- "housing"
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication"
# ============================================================================


# ---- The estimator -------------------------------------------------------------
# A verbatim copy of R/housing/_tools.R in the course repository, which builds
# the curve; the downloadable workspace carries the same copy in R/spec_tools.R.

# The same code runs in the downloadable workspace and in webR on the browser
# lab, so all three give the same numbers. The standard errors and the average
# marginal effect come from packages: parameters with sandwich for the HC2
# errors of the linear model, marginaleffects for the average marginal effect
# of the logit. R/housing/check_parity.R in the course repository checks both
# against estimatr and margins. The rows are chosen with dplyr, because
# datawizard evaluates its conditions in a fresh environment and so cannot see
# the arguments of a function.

# The options of the curve, in menu order. Anything else is refused by
# check_spec() with the reason recorded in data/menu_options.csv.
SPEC_AXES <- list(
  comparison = c("white", "nonhispanic"),
  population = c("replies", "all"),
  uncoded    = c("drop", "not_named"),
  model      = c("lpm", "logit"),
  adjust     = c("none", "email", "place", "place_ethnic")
)

# Covariates of each adjustment set; all are recorded before the emails went out.
ADJUST_TERMS <- list(
  none         = character(0),
  email        = "hard_email",
  place        = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third"),
  place_ethnic = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")
)

# The analysed rows and the outcome of one specification. Bounced emails never
# reached an official and are outside the experiment under every option.
spec_frame <- function(audit, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") {
  audit |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply),
                  .env$comparison == "nonhispanic" | group %in% c("white", "hispanic"),
                  .env$population == "all" | reply == 1) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
      y = dplyr::case_when(reply == 0 ~ 0,
                           is.na(named) & .env$uncoded == "not_named" ~ 0,
                           .default = named)
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(y))
}

# The conversion rules of Multi100 (standard_correlation_coefficient.R in
# github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100): t with its df, which is the rule of
# effectsize::t_to_r(); z with the sample size standing in for the missing df;
# a chi-square read as the square of a z, so it carries no sign.
r_multi100 <- function(stat, stat_type, df, n) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    stat_type == "t" ~ effectsize::t_to_r(stat, df, ci = NULL)$r,
    stat_type == "z" ~ tanh(abs(stat) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3))) * sign(stat),
    stat_type == "chi2" ~ tanh(sqrt(abs(stat)) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3)))
  )
}

check_spec <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  chosen <- list(comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
                 model = model, adjust = adjust)
  bad <- names(chosen)[!purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, SPEC_AXES[names(chosen)], \(v, ok) v %in% ok)]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("Not on the curve: ", paste0(bad, " = '", unlist(chosen[bad]), "'", collapse = ", "),
         ". The options are listed in data/menu_options.csv.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# One specification: estimate in percentage points (negative = Hispanic names
# greeted by name less often, the direction of the claim), its SE and 95%
# interval, the test of the model that the specification fits, and the partial
# correlation by the Multi100 rule.
fit_spec <- function(audit, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none") {
  check_spec(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
  terms <- ADJUST_TERMS[[adjust]]
  # only the model columns, and only the emails with every covariate;
  # marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
  frame <- spec_frame(audit, comparison, population, uncoded) |>
    dplyr::select("y", "hisp", dplyr::all_of(terms)) |>
    stats::na.omit()
  form <- stats::reformulate(c("hisp", terms), response = "y")

  if (model == "lpm") {
    fit <- stats::lm(form, data = frame)
    # HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from sandwich::vcovHC() (Zeileis
    # 2004, Journal of Statistical Software), with the t test on the residual df
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "t", stat = row$t,
                 df = row$df_error, p = row$p)
    est <- list(b = row$Coefficient, se = row$SE, low = row$CI_low, high = row$CI_high)
  } else {
    fit <- stats::glm(form, family = stats::binomial(), data = frame)
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, ci_method = "wald")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "z", stat = row$z,
                 df = NA_real_, p = row$p)
    # The average marginal effect: the mean over the analysed emails of the
    # predicted probability with a Hispanic name minus that with a comparison
    # name, with delta-method errors (marginaleffects; Arel-Bundock, Greifer and
    # Heiss 2024, Journal of Statistical Software)
    ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
    est <- list(b = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error, low = ame$conf.low, high = ame$conf.high)
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
    model = model, adjust = adjust,
    b_pp = 100 * est$b, se_pp = 100 * est$se,
    coef = test$coef, coef_se = test$coef_se,
    stat_type = test$stat_type, stat = test$stat, df = test$df, p = test$p,
    r = r_multi100(test$stat, test$stat_type, test$df, nrow(frame)),
    n = nrow(frame), n_hisp = sum(frame$hisp == 1), n_comp = sum(frame$hisp == 0),
    rate_hisp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 1]),
    rate_comp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 0]),
    ci_low = 100 * est$low, ci_high = 100 * est$high
  )
}

# The free-text label that carries a specification to the class chart.
spec_line <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  sprintf("comparison=%s population=%s uncoded=%s model=%s adjust=%s",
          comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
}


# ---- The menu --------------------------------------------------------------------
# The eleven decisions in the order of the menu, each with the options that the
# curve keeps. The five decisions of SPEC_AXES keep two or more options, which
# multiply to the 64 specifications; on the other six the curve keeps one.
# Every other option is a row of data/menu_options.csv, whose reason the
# helpers print when it is asked for.
.menu <- list(
  # Level 1 – Estimands
  outcome    = "named",
  comparison = SPEC_AXES$comparison,
  population = SPEC_AXES$population,
  names      = "both",
  officials  = "any",
  # Level 2 – Measurement
  uncoded    = SPEC_AXES$uncoded,
  bounced    = "exclude",
  # Level 3 – Estimation
  model      = SPEC_AXES$model,
  adjust     = SPEC_AXES$adjust,
  inference  = "model",
  scale      = "pp"
)
.level_titles <- c(estimand    = "Level 1 – Estimands",
                   measurement = "Level 2 – Measurement",
                   estimation  = "Level 3 – Estimation")


# ---- The shipped files -----------------------------------------------------------
# Each file is read once and cached. The base reader keeps this code identical,
# line for line, with the copy in R/spec_tools.R of the workspace. An empty cell must read as
# NA, as readr reads it: the 14 authorities without community thirds would
# otherwise enter the adjusted models as a fourth level "".
.cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.read_once <- function(name, path) {
  if (is.null(.cache[[name]])) {
    if (!file.exists(path))
      stop(sprintf("%s is missing – the page loads it through its resources list. Reload the page.",
                   path), call. = FALSE)
    assign(name, utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8", # r-style: keep – the same reader as the workspace
                                 na.strings = c("", "NA")),
           envir = .cache)
  }
  .cache[[name]]
}
.audit   <- function() .read_once("audit", "data/housing_audit.csv")
.curve   <- function() .read_once("curve", "data/spec_curve.csv")
.options <- function() .read_once("options", "data/menu_options.csv")


# ---- Pages of the course site ----------------------------------------------------
.pages <- c(
  "cases/housing/index.qmd"       = "Case study",
  "cases/housing/menu.qmd"        = "Specification menu",
  "cases/housing/map.qmd"         = "Decision map",
  "cases/housing/multiverse.qmd"  = "Multiverse",
  "companion/experiments.qmd"     = "Audit experiments",
  "companion/binary-outcomes.qmd" = "Binary outcomes",
  "companion/dags.qmd"            = "Causal graphs and conditioning",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"      = "The multiverse and its critics")
.page_ref <- function(path) {
  title <- if (path %in% names(.pages)) .pages[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub("\\.qmd$", ".html", path))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}


# ---- Validation ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two entry points into the same rules. .validate() takes a named list, which
# is how try_spec() supplies its arguments; .check_choices() reads the eleven
# my_* choices of the preregistration block. An option that is not on the
# curve stops with the reason from menu_options.csv, the page of the course
# site that teaches it, and the options that stay on the curve.
.on_menu <- function(axis, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[axis]]

.refuse <- function(axis, v, as_args) {
  shown <- if (as_args) axis else paste0("my_", axis)
  keep  <- .menu[[axis]]
  map   <- paste0("  Every decision and its options: ", .page_ref("cases/housing/map.qmd"))
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".", shown, shown, keep[1]),
         call. = FALSE)
  opts <- .options()
  row  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, .data$option == .env$v)
  off  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, !.data$on_curve)$option
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" (%s) is not on the curve of %d specifications, so it has no result here.",
            shown, v, row$label, nrow(.curve())),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    paste0("  Where it is taught: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  To stay on the curve, choose %s = %s.", shown, .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown, v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(keep, collapse = " | ")),
    if (length(off) > 0)
      sprintf("  Off the curve, refused with the reason why: %s.", paste(off, collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(a) .on_menu(a, ch[[a]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], as_args)
  ch[names(.menu)]
}

# The choices are looked up from the frame of this function outwards, which
# reaches the session in which the preregistration block was run.
.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- paste0("my_", names(.menu))
  ch <- mget(need, envir = environment(), inherits = TRUE, ifnotfound = list(NULL))
  missing <- need[purrr::map_lgl(ch, is.null)]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice in the preregistration block and run it first.", call. = FALSE)
  .validate(stats::setNames(ch, names(.menu)))
}


# ---- The live fit ----------------------------------------------------------------
# fit_spec() on the five decisions that vary on the curve, with the 95%
# interval of the estimate that it returns (a t interval from parameters for
# the linear model, a normal interval from marginaleffects for the average
# marginal effect of the logit) and the place of the result among the 64. The
# fit is checked against its row of data/spec_curve.csv; a difference means
# that the page loaded an incomplete file.
.result <- function(ch) {
  fit <- fit_spec(.audit(), ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .curve()
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model,
                          .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1) {
    warning("This specification has no row in data/spec_curve.csv; reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  } else if (abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6 || abs(fit$stat - stored$stat) > 1e-6) {
    warning(sprintf("The live fit (%.4f points, %s = %.4f) differs from the curve that this page loaded (%.4f points, %s = %.4f). Reload the page.",
                    fit$b_pp, fit$stat_type, fit$stat, stored$b_pp, fit$stat_type, stored$stat),
            call. = FALSE)
  }
  c(fit, list(further = sum(curve$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(curve)))
}


# ---- The printout ----------------------------------------------------------------
.comparison_label <- function(comparison)
  c(white = "white names", nonhispanic = "white and Black names")[[comparison]]

.fmt_p <- function(p) sprintf("= %s", format(signif(p, 2), scientific = FALSE))

.class_line <- function(res) {
  below <- res$b_pp < 0
  sig   <- res$p < 0.05
  if (below && sig) "below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim"
  else if (below) "below zero, but not significant at 5%"
  else if (sig) "above zero and significant at 5%, against the direction of the claim"
  else "above zero and not significant at 5%"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL) {
  unit <- if (ch$population == "all") "delivered emails" else "replies"
  test <- if (res$stat_type == "t") c(
    sprintf("  Test: t = %.2f on %d df, p %s (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)",
            res$stat, round(res$df), .fmt_p(res$p))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("  Test: z = %.2f, p %s (logistic regression; the difference is its average marginal effect)",
            res$stat, .fmt_p(res$p)),
    sprintf("        logit coefficient %.3f, standard error %.3f", res$coef, res$coef_se)
  )
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", spec_line(ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust)),
    sprintf("  Greeted by name: Hispanic names %.1f%% of %d %s, %s %.1f%% of %d",
            res$rate_hisp, res$n_hisp, unit, .comparison_label(ch$comparison), res$rate_comp,
            res$n_comp),
    sprintf("  Difference: %.2f percentage points, 95%% interval %.2f to %.2f",
            res$b_pp, res$ci_low, res$ci_high),
    test,
    sprintf("  n = %d %s, partial r = %.3f (the conversion rule of Multi100)", res$n, unit, res$r),
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %d of the %d specifications have an estimate further below zero",
            res$further, res$n_curve)))
  invisible(res)
}


# ---- Task 4: the exploratory helpers -----------------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

# The first five arguments are the decisions on which the curve keeps more
# than one option; the other six are fixed on the curve, and asking for any
# other option of theirs prints the reason why it is not on the curve.
try_spec <- function(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none", outcome = "named", names = "both",
                     officials = "any", bounced = "exclude", inference = "model", scale = "pp") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, comparison = comparison, population = population,
                       names = names, officials = officials, uncoded = uncoded,
                       bounced = bounced, model = model, adjust = adjust,
                       inference = inference, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b_pp = res$b_pp, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,  # r-style: keep – data.frame() spreads the list of choices into columns
                    stat_type = res$stat_type, stat = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", dplyr::bind_rows(.tried$log, row), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The running log of everything try_spec() has fitted. Only the decisions that
# varied are shown; the others are those of the reference specification.
my_experiments <- function() {
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet – call try_spec() at least once.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  varied <- purrr::keep(names(.menu), \(a) dplyr::n_distinct(d[[a]]) > 1)
  show <- d |>
    dplyr::transmute(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(varied)),
                     estimate = round(.data$b_pp, 2),
                     interval = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", .data$ci_low, .data$ci_high),
                     test = sprintf("%s = %.2f", .data$stat_type, .data$stat),
                     p = signif(.data$p, 2),
                     n = .data$n)
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications you have tried (%d), estimates in percentage points:\n", nrow(d)))
  # wide enough for all five varied decisions on one line
  old_width <- options(width = max(getOption("width"), 120))
  on.exit(options(old_width))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nEstimates from %.2f to %.2f points  |  below zero and significant at 5%%: %d of %d",
                     min(d$b_pp), max(d$b_pp), sum(d$b_pp < 0 & d$p < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

submit_exploration <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  if (is.null(.tried$last))
    stop("Nothing to submit – call try_spec() first, ending with the specification you want on the chart.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .submit(.tried$last$ch, .tried$last$res, "explore",
          "Your exploratory submission (the last specification you tried):", nickname)
}


# ---- Task 5: the declared helpers --------------------------------------------------
# prereg() prints the block and returns it, so that run_spec() can check that
# the block has not changed since.
prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  rows <- .options() |>
    dplyr::filter(paste(.data$axis, .data$option) %in% paste(names(ch), unlist(ch))) |>
    dplyr::arrange(match(.data$axis, names(.menu))) |>
    dplyr::mutate(line = sprintf("    %-31s : %-12s (%s)", .data$decision, .data$option, .data$label))
  block <- purrr::imap(.level_titles, \(title, lv) c(paste0("  ", title), rows$line[rows$level == lv])) |>
    unlist(use.names = FALSE)
  ph <- stats::setNames(rows$phrase, rows$axis)
  statement <- c(
    sprintf("%s%s, %s, %s, the difference in the share that drew %s between Hispanic names and %s (%s, %s).",
            toupper(substr(ph[["population"]], 1, 1)), substring(ph[["population"]], 2),
            ph[["names"]], ph[["officials"]], ph[["outcome"]], ph[["comparison"]],
            ph[["uncoded"]], ph[["bounced"]]),
    sprintf("Estimated with %s, %s, tested by %s and reported %s.",
            ph[["model"]], ph[["adjust"]], ph[["inference"]], ph[["scale"]]))
  writeLines(c(
    "DECLARED – your preregistered specification, fixed before it is fitted:",
    "",
    block,
    "",
    "  The estimand statement",
    strwrap(statement, width = 78, indent = 4, exdent = 4),
    "",
    "run_spec() and report_result() read these choices from here. Rendered into",
    "your report, this block is your preregistration, and it sits above the",
    "cells that fit and submit this specification."))
  invisible(structure(list(choices = ch), class = "housing_prereg"))
}

run_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "housing_prereg"))
    stop("Pass the object that prereg() returned: my_spec <- prereg(), then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!identical(spec$choices, .check_choices()))
    stop("The preregistration block has changed since prereg() returned this object. Run the whole block again, then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  .print_result(spec$choices, .result(spec$choices), "Your preregistered specification, fitted live:")
}

report_result <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  .submit(ch, .result(ch), "declared",
          "Your declared submission (straight from your preregistration):", nickname)
}


# ---- Submission tags ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Both submissions of a participant carry one short tag inside the spec label,
# "explore: [amber-otter-42] housing …", so that the participant can find
# their own marks on the class chart. The same functions sit in
# R/spec_tools.R of the workspace, which keeps the tag in a file; here it
# lasts for the browser session, and a nickname passed to either submission
# function sets it or brings it back after a reload.
.tag_words <- list(
  adj  = c("amber", "azure", "bright", "calm", "coral", "crisp", "dusky", "early",
           "fair", "gentle", "golden", "hazel", "ivory", "jade", "keen", "lively",
           "lunar", "misty", "noble", "olive", "pale", "quiet", "rapid", "rosy",
           "russet", "silver", "snowy", "solar", "sunny", "swift", "velvet", "vivid"),
  noun = c("otter", "heron", "lynx", "badger", "finch", "hare", "ibex", "kestrel",
           "lark", "marten", "newt", "owl", "puffin", "quail", "raven", "seal",
           "stoat", "tern", "vole", "wren", "bison", "crane", "dove", "egret",
           "fox", "gecko", "koala", "lemur", "moose", "panda", "robin", "swan")
)
.tag_env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("tag", NULL, envir = .tag_env)

# A fresh tag, drawn without touching the random-number stream of the session.
.new_tag <- function() {
  had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  if (had_seed) old_seed <- get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
  on.exit(if (had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = globalenv())
          else rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()))
  set.seed(as.integer((as.numeric(Sys.time()) * 1000) %% 1e9) + Sys.getpid() %% 1e5)
  paste(sample(.tag_words$adj, 1), sample(.tag_words$noun, 1), sample(10:99, 1), sep = "-")
}

# A nickname reduced to lower-case ASCII letters, digits and single hyphens,
# at most 24 characters – the only form that the class chart parses.
.clean_tag <- function(x) {
  # iconv on Windows turns these into "?": the Romanian comma-below letters and the eszett
  x <- gsub("ß", "ss", chartr("ȘșȚț", "SsTt", trimws(as.character(x)[1])))
  ascii <- suppressWarnings(iconv(x, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"))
  if (!is.na(ascii)) x <- ascii
  x <- gsub("^-+|-+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x)))
  x <- gsub("-+$", "", substr(x, 1, 24))
  if (is.na(x) || !nzchar(x))
    stop("A nickname needs at least one letter or digit, for example nickname = \"blue-heron\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  x
}

# The tag of this session: the nickname if one is given, otherwise the tag
# already drawn, otherwise a fresh one. Returns the tag and the one it replaced.
.class_tag <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  stored <- .tag_env$tag
  tag <- if (!is.null(nickname)) .clean_tag(nickname) else if (!is.null(stored)) stored else .new_tag()
  assign("tag", tag, envir = .tag_env)
  list(tag = tag, replaced = if (!is.null(stored) && !identical(tag, stored)) stored)
}

# One submission, used by both phases. The phase, the tag and the word of the
# case are prefixed to the free-text spec label, which carries the five
# decisions that vary on the curve. The estimate and its standard error are
# sent in percentage points, the statistic of the model in the t field (a z
# for a logit, whose df field stays empty), and r by the rule of Multi100.
.submit <- function(ch, res, phase, lead, nickname = NULL) {
  tg <- .class_tag(nickname)
  spec_label <- paste0(phase, ": [", tg$tag, "] ", .case_word, " ",
                       spec_line(ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust))
  value <- c(spec = spec_label, b = sprintf("%.5f", res$b_pp), se = sprintf("%.5f", res$se_pp),
             t = sprintf("%.3f", res$stat), df = if (is.na(res$df)) "" else as.character(round(res$df)),
             n = as.character(res$n), r = sprintf("%.3f", res$r))
  query <- purrr::imap_chr(.form_entry, \(entry, k)
    paste0(entry, "=", utils::URLencode(value[[k]], reserved = TRUE))) |>
    paste(collapse = "&")
  url <- sprintf("https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/%s/viewform?usp=pp_url&%s", .form_id, query)

  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    "",
    paste("  spec:", spec_label),
    sprintf("  b = %s | se = %s | %s = %s | df = %s | n = %d | r = %s",
            value[["b"]], value[["se"]], res$stat_type, value[["t"]],
            if (nzchar(value[["df"]])) value[["df"]] else "(none, a logit)", res$n, value[["r"]]),
    "  (b and se in percentage points)",
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    "",
    "Open the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every field",
    "pre-filled; just press Send.",
    "",
    url))
  if (requireNamespace("htmltools", quietly = TRUE))
    print(htmltools::tags$p(htmltools::tags$a(href = url, target = "_blank",
                                              "Open the pre-filled form in a new tab")))
  writeLines(c(
    "",
    sprintf("Your marks on the class chart carry the tag %s%s.", tg$tag,
            if (!is.null(tg$replaced)) sprintf(" (it replaces %s)", tg$replaced) else ""),
    sprintf("Look for it on the Multiverse page, %s/cases/housing/multiverse.html.", .course_url),
    "Both of your submissions share it while this page stays open; after a reload,",
    sprintf("bring it back with nickname = \"%s\". To choose your own, pass a", tg$tag),
    "nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public."))
  invisible(list(spec = spec_label, tag = tg$tag, b = res$b_pp, se = res$se_pp, statistic = res$stat,
                 df = res$df, n = res$n, r = res$r, url = url))
}
```

Five analysts reanalysed a claim of the housing-audit case [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] for the Multi100 project [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; you are analyst no. 6. The claim is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts", in the words of the original authors (OAs) as the SCORE programme selected them. The [exercise overview](exercise.qmd) sets out the five tasks, and the [case study](index.qmd) the original study, Multi100 and the five reanalyses.

The five tasks take you from a setup check to two marks on the live class chart, one submitted while you explore the menu in Task 4 and one that you declare in your preregistration in Task 5 before running it. The page of your track says which tasks your session covers, and whether it sends anything to the class chart. Every fit on this page is live: the estimator of the course runs in your browser, on the same file and with the same code as in the workspace.

## Warm-up – the three Rs {#warm-up}

The warm-up settles the vocabulary before you touch any data. Three of the four scenarios below describe one of our three Rs – reproducibility, robustness, replicability – and the fourth describes something else. Read all four, then label each one in the code cell.

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer runs the Stata `.do` file of the OAs on their public data file and gets a coefficient for Hispanic names that differs from the one printed in the paper, because the public file holds the size, poverty and ethnic composition of each community in thirds rather than as the census values. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though the numbers do not match.

***Scenario 2:*** An analyst takes the same public file, re-implements the analysis in R instead of Stata, and also counts the five replies that carry no greeting code as replies without a greeting. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team emails 3,050 public housing authorities with four new names and finds no difference in how often the replies greet the sender by name. Their conclusion is that the original finding has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Another researcher asks whether the same bias appears when people telephone school districts rather than email housing authorities, codes recorded voice messages instead of written replies, and finds the same pattern. The researcher concludes that the original finding \_\_\_\_\_\_ to another service and another medium.

Fill in the gaps in the code cell below and run it to print your answers back.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap
writeLines(c(
  "Scenario 1: This is an example of ______.",
  "Scenario 2: Is this a case of ______ or ______?",
  "Scenario 3: The original finding has failed to ______.",
  "Scenario 4: The original finding ______ to another service and another medium."
))
```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers

1.  **reproducibility** – rerunning the code of the OAs on their data. The numbers differ, but the activity is still reproduction, and the difference has a documented cause: the blinded file.
2.  a grey area. Re-implementing on the same data in different software is still **reproducibility**, but recoding the uncoded replies is an analytic choice, which makes it a test of **robustness**.
3.  **replicability** – the same question asked of independent new data.
4.  **generalises** (generalisability) – the odd one out, with a new population, new data and a new measure at once.
:::
::::

## Task 2 – The data {#task-2-data}

The **housing-audit data** (`housing_audit.csv`) are already loaded for you as `audit`, one row per email. The file is built from the public file of the OAs on Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU, released under CC0), with plainer column names; the downloadable workspace contains the same file. Run the cell below to count what came back. Edit it freely – this is your environment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# How many emails, and what came back?
audit |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails    = n(),
                           bounced   = sum(is.na(reply)),
                           delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
                           replies   = sum(reply %in% 1),
                           coded     = sum(!is.na(named)))
```

You should find **1,014 emails** (the paper reports 1,017, three more than the public file holds), of which **23 bounced** and never reached an official, **991 delivered**, **563 replies**, and **558 replies with a greeting code**. The column `reply` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and missing for a bounced email. `named` is 1 when a reply greeted the sender by name, 0 when it did not, and missing for every email without a reply and for the five replies that carry no greeting code. The [codebook](data/housing_audit_codebook.md) describes every column.

Now the replies and the greetings by the group of the name, and the share of greetings by name for each of the six names:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(delivered   = n(),
                           replies     = sum(reply == 1),
                           coded       = sum(!is.na(named)),
                           greeted     = sum(named %in% 1),
                           greeted_pct = round(100 * sum(named %in% 1) / sum(!is.na(named)), 1),
                           by = "group")

# The share greeted by name for each of the six names, from the lowest, drawn
# with tinyplot (McDermott, Arel-Bundock and Zeileis; CRAN,
# doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.tinyplot)
greeted <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name")) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("greeted_pct") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                                         labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")))

tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted_pct ~ name | group, data = greeted,
                   type = tinyplot::type_barplot(xlevels = greeted$name, width = 0.7, drop.zeros = TRUE), flip = TRUE,
                   palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"), fill = "by",
                   legend = list("right!", title = "Names meant to indicate"),
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)",
                   ylim = c(0, 72), theme = "minimal")
# the share at the end of each bar
tinyplot::tinyplot(x = seq_len(nrow(greeted)), y = greeted$greeted_pct, flip = TRUE,
                   type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = sprintf("%.1f%%", greeted$greeted_pct), pos = 4),
                   cex = 0.9, add = TRUE)
```

The replies to white names greeted the sender by name in 61.1% of cases, those to Hispanic names in 41.2%: a gap of about 20 points, the size of the published estimate. Black names fall in between, at 56.1%, and of the six names Santiago received the fewest greetings by name.

## Task 2, continued – The estimand and the graph {#task-2-estimand-and-graph}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template that you can adapt:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is, for each housing authority, the difference between whether it would come back with a reply that greets the sender by name to an email signed with a Hispanic name and to the same email signed with a white name. The **target population** is the public housing authorities that received an email.

There is a catch in that sentence. An authority whose official would not reply to one of the names has no greeting to compare. The comparison can then count every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting, or count the replies only, which compares the authorities that replied to Hispanic names with those that replied to white names. These need not be the same authorities.

A causal graph makes the catch visible. A graph of this kind is a diagram of what causes what: variables are nodes, arrows run from cause to effect, and the rules for reading the graph say which paths between the name and the greeting are open, given what the comparison conditions on. The graph below is written in ordinary R, one arrow per string, each written the way it is drawn: `"name -> reply"` is the arrow from the name to the reply. The name can affect whether the official replies, and only a reply can greet the sender by name. Something about the official that nobody recorded (workload, habits of courtesy, attitudes) affects both whether they reply and how they greet, and so does the community of the housing authority. One arrow is switched off with a `#`: the arrow from the name to the greeting, which is the effect on tone that the claim is about.

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Graph machinery for Task 2. make_dag() reads a graph from its arrows, and
# plot_dag() draws it with tinyplot. adjustmentSets() and paths() print the
# answers of dagitty, the R package that the workspace uses, from
# data/dag_answers.csv: R/housing/07_dag_answers.R in the course repository
# computes them with dagitty for every graph to which the graph cell below
# leads. dagitty itself cannot run on this page, because its graph algorithms
# need a JavaScript engine that a browser grants only to a page served with
# cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP), and the course site does not
# send them. Another graph, or another question, goes to dagitty in the
# downloadable workspace. The table arrives with the page through its
# `resources:` list.
.dag_answers <- utils::read.csv("data/dag_answers.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
                                na.strings = "NA")
.dag_elsewhere <- c(
  "This page holds the answers that dagitty gives to the questions of Task 2, for the",
  "graph of the cell with and without the arrow \"name -> greeting\". For another graph",
  "or another question, use the downloadable workspace, where R/dag_starter.R builds",
  "the graph and dagitty answers whatever you ask of it.")

# Where each node sits in the figure, with y counted upwards: the name on the
# left, the greeting on the right, the reply above the line between them. A
# node without a position here is drawn on a row below the graph.
.dag_xy <- list(name = c(0, 0), reply = c(1.5, 1.6), greeting = c(3, 0),
                community = c(2, 0.65), official = c(3, 1.6))

# A graph from arrows written "cause -> effect", one per string. The named
# arguments come last, so that switching off the last arrow with a # never
# leaves a comma dangling. The arrows, sorted, are the key under which
# data/dag_answers.csv holds the answers for the graph.
make_dag <- function(..., exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official") {
  arrows <- c(...)
  edges <- purrr::map(arrows, \(a) {
    ends <- trimws(strsplit(a, "->", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
    if (length(ends) < 2 || !all(nzchar(ends)) || grepl("<-", a, fixed = TRUE))
      stop(sprintf("Write each arrow as \"cause -> effect\", for example \"name -> reply\"; \"%s\" is not one.",
                   a), call. = FALSE)
    data.frame(from = ends[-length(ends)], to = ends[-1])
  }) |>
    dplyr::bind_rows() |>
    dplyr::distinct()
  structure(list(edges = edges, nodes = unique(c(exposure, outcome, edges$from, edges$to)),
                 exposure = exposure, outcome = outcome, latent = latent,
                 key = paste(sort(paste(edges$from, "->", edges$to), method = "radix"),
                             collapse = "; ")),
            class = "simple_dag")
}

# The minimal adjustment sets for the total effect of the exposure on the
# outcome, as dagitty::adjustmentSets() returns them, read from the table. The
# rows are chosen with dplyr, because datawizard cannot see the arguments of a
# function.
adjustmentSets <- function(x, exposure = x$exposure, outcome = x$outcome, effect = "total", ...) {
  rows <- dplyr::filter(.dag_answers, .data$call == "adjustmentSets", .data$arrows %in% x$key,
                        .data$exposure %in% paste(.env$exposure, collapse = ", "),
                        .data$outcome %in% paste(.env$outcome, collapse = ", "),
                        .data$latent %in% paste(sort(x$latent, method = "radix"), collapse = ", "),
                        .data$effect %in% .env$effect)
  if (nrow(rows) == 0) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  structure(strsplit(rows$answer[rows$item > 0], ", ", fixed = TRUE), class = "simple_dag_sets")
}

print.simple_dag_sets <- function(x, ...) {
  shown <- if (length(x) == 0) "(no set of observed variables closes every backdoor path)" else
    purrr::map_chr(x, \(z) if (length(z) > 0) paste0("{ ", paste(z, collapse = ", "), " }") else "{}")
  writeLines(shown)
  invisible(x)
}

# Registered rather than left in the session: these cells do not evaluate in
# the global environment, so plain S3 dispatch would not find the method.
registerS3method("print", "simple_dag_sets", print.simple_dag_sets)

# The paths between the exposure and the outcome, each with its arrows, and
# whether it is open given the conditioning set Z, as dagitty::paths() returns
# them, read from the table.
paths <- function(x, from = x$exposure, to = x$outcome, Z = character(0), ...) {
  rows <- dplyr::filter(.dag_answers, .data$call == "paths", .data$arrows %in% x$key,
                        .data$exposure %in% paste(.env$from, collapse = ", "),
                        .data$outcome %in% paste(.env$to, collapse = ", "),
                        .data$latent %in% paste(sort(x$latent, method = "radix"), collapse = ", "),
                        .data$Z %in% paste(sort(unique(as.character(unlist(.env$Z))), method = "radix"),
                                           collapse = ", "))
  if (nrow(rows) == 0) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  list(paths = rows$answer, open = rows$open)
}

# The figure. Colour marks the exposure and the outcome, and the official,
# whom nobody observed, is drawn pale. Each arrow stops at the edge of the box
# of its target.
.dag_parts <- function(d) {
  at <- \(v, k) if (v %in% names(.dag_xy)) .dag_xy[[v]][k] else NA_real_
  list(nodes = tibble::tibble(name = d$nodes, x = purrr::map_dbl(d$nodes, \(v) at(v, 1)),
                              y = purrr::map_dbl(d$nodes, \(v) at(v, 2))),
       edges = d$edges, exposure = d$exposure, outcome = d$outcome, latent = d$latent)
}

plot_dag <- function(d) {
  parts <- .dag_parts(d)
  nodes <- parts$nodes |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      unplaced = is.na(.data$x),
      x = dplyr::if_else(.data$unplaced, 1.2 * (cumsum(.data$unplaced) - 1), .data$x),
      y = dplyr::if_else(.data$unplaced, -0.9, .data$y),
      half_w = 0.06 + 0.032 * nchar(.data$name),
      role = factor(dplyr::case_when(.data$name %in% parts$exposure ~ "exposure",
                                     .data$name %in% parts$outcome ~ "outcome",
                                     .data$name %in% parts$latent ~ "unobserved",
                                     .default = "observed"),
                    levels = c("exposure", "outcome", "observed", "unobserved")))
  # how far along a unit vector (ux, uy) the edge of a box of half-width w lies
  to_edge <- \(ux, uy, w) pmin(w / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), 0.15 / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9))
  tails <- dplyr::select(nodes, from = "name", x0 = "x", y0 = "y", w0 = "half_w")
  heads <- dplyr::select(nodes, to = "name", x1 = "x", y1 = "y", w1 = "half_w")
  arrows <- parts$edges |>
    dplyr::inner_join(tails, by = "from") |>
    dplyr::inner_join(heads, by = "to") |>
    dplyr::mutate(len = sqrt((.data$x1 - .data$x0)^2 + (.data$y1 - .data$y0)^2),
                  ux = (.data$x1 - .data$x0) / .data$len,
                  uy = (.data$y1 - .data$y0) / .data$len,
                  s0 = to_edge(.data$ux, .data$uy, .data$w0),
                  s1 = to_edge(.data$ux, .data$uy, .data$w1) + 0.04,
                  x = .data$x0 + .data$s0 * .data$ux, y = .data$y0 + .data$s0 * .data$uy,
                  xend = .data$x1 - .data$s1 * .data$ux, yend = .data$y1 - .data$s1 * .data$uy)

  # the boxes, coloured by role; tinyplot has no type for arrows, so they go
  # on the same canvas through graphics::arrows(); then the names, white on
  # the coloured boxes and dark on the pale one
  tinyplot::tinyplot(xmin = nodes$x - 0.8 * nodes$half_w, xmax = nodes$x + 0.8 * nodes$half_w,
                     ymin = nodes$y - 0.1, ymax = nodes$y + 0.1, by = nodes$role, type = "rect",
                     palette = c("#1b6ca8", "#d1495b", "grey45", "grey88"), fill = "by",
                     legend = list("bottom!", title = NULL), axes = FALSE, frame.plot = FALSE,
                     xlab = NA, ylab = NA,
                     xlim = range(nodes$x) + c(-0.45, 0.45), ylim = range(nodes$y) + c(-0.3, 0.3),
                     grid = FALSE, theme = "minimal")
  graphics::arrows(arrows$x, arrows$y, arrows$xend, arrows$yend,
                   length = 0.1, angle = 20, col = "grey40", lwd = 1.5)
  tinyplot::tinyplot(x = nodes$x, y = nodes$y, by = nodes$role,
                     type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = nodes$name, font = 2),
                     palette = c("white", "white", "white", "grey25"), cex = 0.85, add = TRUE)
}
```

`make_dag()`, `adjustmentSets()`, `paths()` and `plot_dag()` are already available on this page, so you can go straight to the graph. In the downloadable workspace the two questions go to `dagitty`, the R package for causal graphs, which cannot run on this page. Here `adjustmentSets()` and `paths()` print the answers that dagitty gives, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty for the graph of the cell below, with and without the arrow of the claim ([codebook](data/dag_answers_codebook.md)). Any other graph gets a pointer to the workspace.

Now build the graph and put two questions to it. The first is what has to be adjusted for when the comparison counts every delivered email. The second is which paths from the name to the greeting are open once the comparison is made among replies only, which is what `Z = "reply"` asks: it conditions on the reply.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
my_dag <- make_dag(
  # The name can affect whether the official replies at all.
  "name -> reply",
  # Only a reply can greet the sender by name.
  "reply -> greeting",
  # The official, whom nobody observed, affects both the reply and the greeting.
  "official -> reply",
  "official -> greeting",
  # So does the community of the housing authority, held in thirds in the data.
  "community -> reply",
  "community -> greeting",

  # The effect on tone that the claim is about: take the # off if you believe it.
  # "name -> greeting",

  exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official"
)

adjustmentSets(my_dag)       # r-style: keep – the function of this page, which reads the answers of dagitty
paths(my_dag, Z = "reply")   # r-style: keep – the function of this page, which reads the answers of dagitty
plot_dag(my_dag)
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns `{}`, the empty set: nothing has to be adjusted for, because nothing points into the name. The names were assigned at random, so no common cause of the name and the greeting can exist. Conditioning on the reply changes the picture. The path through the reply closes, but two paths open, one through the community and one through the official, because the reply is a common effect of the name and of each of them (a collider), and comparing replies only conditions on it. This is the problem of conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, which @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias sets out for audit experiments.

Now take the `#` off the arrow `"name -> greeting"`, run the cell again, then run the cell below, which also adjusts for the community. Answer three questions for your own notes: why the adjustment set stays empty; which paths stay open among replies once the community is adjusted for, and what that means for a gap among replies; and which emails keep the comparison randomised.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
paths(my_dag, Z = c("reply", "community"))  # r-style: keep – the function of this page, which reads the answers of dagitty
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers

1.  The set stays `{}` because nothing points into the name, whatever arrows leave it: the names were randomised.
2.  The direct path and the path through the official stay open. A gap among replies mixes the effect of the name on tone with differences between the officials who reply to each name, and adjusting for the community cannot remove the second, because the official is unobserved.
3.  Every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting. That comparison estimates the effect of the name on receiving a greeting by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply.

The difference between the two comparisons is the decision on which emails are counted, the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and whatever you conclude here belongs in field 4 of your preregistration in Task 5.
:::

## Task 3 – The reproduction {#task-3-reproduction}

This is the **reproducibility** check. Five analysts reanalysed the claim for Multi100, each with code of their own, and Multi100 recorded a test statistic for four of them. Choose one of the five and reproduce the analysis from the public file of the OAs, `audit_original.csv`, which keeps their column names. `Response_Dichotomous` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and empty for a bounced email. `ProperName` is the greeting by name, empty for every email that has no reply with a greeting code. `TreatmentGroup` holds the group and the sex of the name (`"Hispanic male"`, `"white female"` and so on).

| Analyst | What the analysis compared | Emails counted | Test | Recorded by Multi100 |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [8PTRZ](#task-3-8ptrz) | Hispanic names against all other names | the 558 replies with a greeting code | chi-square test of a 2 × 2 table | $\chi^2$ = 14.265 |
| [UYV3F](#task-3-uyv3f) | Hispanic against white names | the 362 coded replies to those names | logistic regression without covariates | z = −3.771 |
| [EWFMI](#task-3-ewfmi) | the three groups, with Hispanic names as the base | the 549 coded replies that carry a poverty third | logistic regression with the sex of the name, the poverty third and the hard-to-find address | z = 3.645 |
| [25N5D](#task-3-25n5d) | Hispanic against white names | the 665 delivered emails to those names, a missing reply counted as no greeting | two-proportion test | $\chi^2$ = 13.683 |
| [P9W8Y](#task-3-p9w8y) | the three groups | the 558 replies with a greeting code | likelihood-ratio test of a logistic regression | none |

Each analyst has a cell of their own below, and each cell is an exercise: replace the blank (`______`) with the missing code, then press "Run Code". A hint and the full solution sit under every cell. When you have your value, type the analyst and the value into the chat, for example `UYV3F z = -3.771`, hold it, and send it on the facilitator's word. The course computes the same five refits in its own pipeline, with the same functions, and the four recorded statistics all come out exactly ([`analysts5.csv`](data/analysts5_codebook.md)). For P9W8Y Multi100 recorded no statistic, so its analysis can be run again but there is nothing on record to match it against.

## Solution

original <- utils::read.csv("data/audit_original.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
replies_p9w8y <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>

m_p9w8y <- glm(ProperName ~ ethnicity, family = binomial(), data = replies_p9w8y)

anova(update(m_p9w8y, . ~ 1), m_p9w8y, test = "LRT")

### Defaults and codings {#task-3-defaults}

Now find out why your number is exactly that number. For a 2 × 2 table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the continuity correction of Yates unless they are told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by 0.5 before squaring, a remedy designed for small tables. Neither 8PTRZ nor 25N5D asked for the correction. The defaults of the two functions applied it, and the recorded values are the corrected ones. The cell below runs both tests without the correction.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
original <- utils::read.csv("data/audit_original.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download

# 8PTRZ: the replies with a greeting code, Hispanic against all other names
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)  # r-style: keep – the table that chisq.test() takes
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)

# 25N5D: the delivered emails, Hispanic against white names
counts_25n5d <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(Response_Dichotomous) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup),
                          greeted = Response_Dichotomous == 1 & ProperName %in% 1) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greetings = sum(greeted), emails = n(), by = "hispanic_name")
prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails, correct = FALSE)
```

Without the correction the two statistics are 14.95 and 14.33. Neither changes the conclusion, but only the corrected values match the record, and the description "a chi-square test" fits both. The coding of the data matters in the same way. The z of EWFMI is positive and the z of UYV3F negative, although both describe Hispanic names greeted by name less often, because EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, so that the coefficient compares white names with Hispanic names. A reproduction needs the code, or at least every default and every coding on which the code relied.

The scripts that the analysts submitted are on the OSF, in the Multi100 component of the paper ([osf.io/38rsh](https://osf.io/38rsh/)), one sub-component for each analyst: 8PTRZ [osf.io/j8wvh](https://osf.io/j8wvh/), UYV3F [osf.io/3672s](https://osf.io/3672s/) (a review document only), EWFMI [osf.io/jhvca](https://osf.io/jhvca/), 25N5D [osf.io/v8zah](https://osf.io/v8zah/) and P9W8Y [osf.io/pzwbm](https://osf.io/pzwbm/).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproduction and the five analysts

You reproduced the value of the analyst whom you chose, and so did everyone else who chose the same analyst, because everyone ran the same code on the same file. This is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish.

The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for this claim. Three concluded that the results were evidence for the claim and two that they were evidence neither for nor against it, although the four statistics that Multi100 recorded all come from gaps in the same direction. Part of the difference lies in the questions that each analyst chose to answer (which names to compare, which emails to count), and part in what each analyst took to count as evidence: one of the two who answered 'neither' found the gap but judged it substantially smaller than the published one. The [case study](index.qmd) sets out what each analyst chose.
:::

## Task 4 – The menu {#task-4-menu}

This task is **exploratory**. You try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing in this task is preregistered; the preregistration comes in Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and every argument defaults to the reference specification, the raw gap of the paper: Hispanic against white names, among the replies, the five uncoded replies left out, a difference in proportions without covariates. So changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it was. Every call is a live fit in your browser.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Nothing changed – the reference specification.
try_spec()
```

The printout gives the shares greeted by name in the two groups, the difference in percentage points with its 95% interval, the test of the model (a *t* with HC2 standard errors for the linear model, the *z* of the logit coefficient for the logit), the number of emails analysed, the partial *r* by the conversion rule of Multi100, the class of the result, and its place among the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim.

Each of the five calls below changes a single decision. The first two change the question that is being asked of the data, the third changes how the outcome is measured, and the last two change only how the same question is estimated. Run them and compare the results.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(comparison = "nonhispanic")     # Hispanic names against white and Black names together
try_spec(population = "all")             # every delivered email, no reply counted as no greeting
try_spec(uncoded    = "not_named")       # the five uncoded replies counted as no greeting
try_spec(model      = "logit")           # the model of the paper, as an average marginal effect
try_spec(adjust     = "place_ethnic")    # the covariates of the original model, in thirds
```

The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, so trying one is part of the exercise. The helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve and names the page of the course that teaches it, and the [decision map](map.qmd) sets out every decision and its options on one page. Run the cell, then edit it to try others, such as `outcome = "reply"`, `names = "male"`, `comparison = "black"`, `adjust = "acs_continuous"` or `inference = "one_tailed"`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# An option that is not on the curve: the helper refuses it and says why.
try_spec(model = "three_group")
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, each with the reference specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  # the five decisions on which the curve keeps more than one option
  comparison = "white",      # white | nonhispanic          off the curve: black
  population = "replies",    # replies | all
  uncoded    = "drop",       # drop | not_named
  model      = "lpm",        # lpm | logit                  off the curve: three_group
  adjust     = "none",       # none | email | place | place_ethnic
                             #                              off the curve: name_sex | acs_continuous
  # the six decisions that are fixed on the curve
  outcome    = "named",      # named                        off the curve: reply | reply24
  names      = "both",       # both                         off the curve: male | female
  officials  = "any",        # any                          off the curve: hispanic
  bounced    = "exclude",    # exclude                      off the curve: no_reply
  inference  = "model",      # model                        off the curve: randomisation | chisq | one_tailed
  scale      = "pp"          # pp                           off the curve: odds_ratio | r
)
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to view the small multiverse that you have just built. It shows only the decisions that you varied, so the differences are easy to read:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so that it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live [Multiverse]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) chart as an open circle, labelled **exploratory**, and marked with the tag that the cell prints, such as `amber-otter-42`. The tag is how you find your own marks on the chart, and your declared result in Task 5 carries the same one. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exploratory and declared

Because you chose this specification after finding out what several specifications do, it lacks the guarantee that comes with a choice declared in a preregistration before its result is known: no one can rule out that it was chosen *because* of its result. This is something that we almost never know about published papers, unless their analysis was preregistered and every departure from the preregistration documented. In this course exploration is a natural step, and you also practise preregistering the analysis that you choose, so you submit twice, once here and once in Task 5.
:::

## Task 5 – The preregistration {#task-5-preregistration}

Preregistration means setting out your choice in a plan **before** you know what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. On this page the plan is the preregistration cell below, and it binds mechanically as well: the session remembers the choices that you declare in that cell, and `run_spec()` and `report_result()` read them from there.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## A shortened preregistration

*Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

Make one choice on each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell. The five decisions at Level 1 fix the question that you are asking, the two at Level 2 fix how the outcome is measured, and the four at Level 3 fix how it is estimated. The curve of 64 specifications keeps two or more options on five of these decisions and a single option on the other six. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: housing_audit.csv (1,014 emails, public,
#    CC0); I know that the reference specification gives -19.97 points, and
#    what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 64 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# Level 1 – Estimands (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome    <- "named"     # named   (greeted by name, the outcome of the claim)
my_comparison <- "white"     # white | nonhispanic   (white names, or white and Black names)
my_population <- "replies"   # replies | all   (replies only, or every delivered email)
my_names      <- "both"      # both   (male and female names pooled)
my_officials  <- "any"       # any    (replies from every official)

# Level 2 – Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_uncoded    <- "drop"      # drop | not_named   (the five replies without a greeting code)
my_bounced    <- "exclude"   # exclude   (the 23 emails that never arrived)

# Level 3 – Estimation (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_model      <- "lpm"       # lpm | logit   (difference in proportions, or logistic regression)
my_adjust     <- "none"      # none | email | place | place_ethnic
my_inference  <- "model"     # model   (HC2 t test, or the z test of the logit)
my_scale      <- "pp"        # pp   (percentage points)

# 4. Why this specification answers the claim, in one sentence grounded in
#    the causal graph of Task 2: .............................................
# 5. Supported if the estimate is below zero with p < .05 under the test of
#    the model; undermined if it is not significant or above zero. I will
#    report what I get.

my_spec <- prereg()   # checks every choice, prints your preregistration and keeps it
```

The cell above, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.

## Task 5, continued – Fit, report and place {#task-5-fit-report}

This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you: together the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. `run_spec()` fits your declared specification and prints the same lines as `try_spec()`. It refuses to run if the preregistration cell has changed since `prereg()` read it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_spec)
```

The difference is in percentage points, and a value below zero means that replies to Hispanic names greeted the sender by name less often, the direction of the claim. Whether it is significant is decided by the test of the model, and the line headed `Class:` says which of the four cases your result falls in.

Now send it to the class chart. The submission is built from your declaration, so there is nothing to fill in or transcribe. The cell prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; click it and press **Send**. Your mark joins the live [Multiverse]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) chart within seconds, this time as a filled circle labelled **declared**, carrying the same tag as your exploratory result. If you have reloaded this page since Task 4, the session has forgotten that tag, so pass it back with `report_result(nickname = "your-tag")`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator, who adds your mark to the chart.

Finally, place your result on the curve of the claim: the 64 specifications that the menu keeps, ranked from the most negative estimate, with yours ringed.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
spec_curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
  datawizard::data_arrange("b_pp") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n(),
                          emails = factor(population, levels = c("replies", "all"),
                                          labels = c("replies only", "all delivered emails")))
# Yours, chosen with dplyr, because datawizard cannot see the my_ choices of
# the preregistration cell
mine <- spec_curve |>
  dplyr::filter(comparison == my_comparison, population == my_population, uncoded == my_uncoded,
                model == my_model, adjust == my_adjust)

tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank | emails, data = spec_curve, pch = 16,
                   palette = c("#0e3b6a", "#2b8585"), legend = list("right!", title = "Emails counted"),
                   ylim = c(min(spec_curve$b_pp), 0),
                   xlab = "The 64 specifications, from the most negative estimate",
                   ylab = "Hispanic minus comparison names (points)")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = spec_curve, type = tinyplot::type_hline(h = 0), col = "grey60", add = TRUE)
# your specification, ringed; clim keeps a single ring at the size of cex
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = mine, type = tinyplot::type_points(clim = c(3, 3)),
                   pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2.5, col = "#8b1538", add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

All 64 estimates lie below zero, from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and every one of them is significant at 5% under the test of its model. The two clusters are the two answers to the decision on which emails are counted: counting every delivered email moves the estimate about 5 points towards zero, and no other decision moves it by more than about 2.7 points. Within these data the claim holds under every choice on the menu, and only its size moves. The [Multiverse]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) page sets the class submissions beside this curve.

If you want a second declared specification, edit the preregistration cell, rerun it, then rerun `run_spec(my_spec)`. The chart will still label it declared, so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so wherever you write about the result.

## Taking it home

This page keeps nothing once you refresh it, so work you want to keep belongs in the downloadable workspace. Putting that work under version control and publishing the rendered report is the natural next step. The [Git and GitHub module](../../companion/git-github.qmd) of the companion curriculum explains it click by click.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## The downloadable workspace

The exercise on this page, Tasks 1 to 5, also exists in the downloadable workspace, the folder that you open in your IDE, edit and render offline, and keep after the session. The same folder holds the five reproductions of Task 3 as a script, and a GitHub Actions workflow that renders the report and publishes it to GitHub Pages once the folder is pushed to a GitHub repository whose Pages source is set to GitHub Actions. The folder is maintained in the [`replication-lab-housing`]({{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}) repository, and it is yours to reuse.
:::
